text:
**Plan on about 300 W of solar to refill a 1,000 Wh station in one sunny day.** If you can wait a day or two, 200 W works.

**Rule of thumb:** panel watts ≈ capacity ÷ (peak sun hours × ~0.7-0.75). Panels rarely deliver their rated watts because of heat, sun angle and charging losses.

| Peak sun hours | Panel watts for a full recharge in one day |
|---|---|
| 3 h (winter, cloudy) | ~450 W |
| 4 h | ~340 W |
| 5 h | ~270 W |
| 6 h (summer, Southwest) | ~230 W |

These figures come from [Power Station Runtime Calculator](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/).

**If you use a smaller panel:**
- A 200 W panel gives roughly 600-630 Wh on an average day (4-4.5 sun hours). That refills 1,000 Wh in about 1.5 days ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/), [Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station)).
- A 400 W panel gives about 1,200-1,260 Wh a day, so it can fill the station in a day with some margin.

**Winter is the hard case.** At around 2 peak sun hours in a northern January, a one-day refill takes about 700 W or more ([Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).

**Check before you buy:**
- **Solar input limit:** panels above your station's maximum input add nothing at peak. Many 1,000 Wh stations accept 400-800 W, but entry-level ones may cap at 200 W.
- **Voltage window:** the panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay under the station's maximum input voltage. Exceeding it can damage the station. Series wiring adds voltage.
- **Connector:** most panels use MC4, so confirm an adapter for your station is included.
- **Load while charging:** if you're running devices at the same time, the net charge is slower.
